text: Data gravity is a term Dave McCrory coined back in 2010, and it describes something real, not a metaphor you can argue your way around: as a dataset grows, applications and compute get pulled toward it, the same way mass attracts mass. It's not a preference anyone chooses. It's the direct result of one plain fact — large datasets are expensive and slow to move, while compute is cheap and fast to move. And that asymmetry quietly overrides whatever architecture strategy you wrote down.

Three forces drive this, and all three get worse as data volume grows. Egress cost — every major cloud charges per gigabyte to move data out toward another cloud or the internet, and at terabyte or petabyte scale that's real recurring money. Transfer time — moving multiple terabytes takes hours even on a fast link, and petabytes can take days. And operational inertia — once a dataset has pipelines, access controls, and backups built around its location, all of that has to be re-validated after any move.

Put those three together and the cheapest, fastest, least risky option for almost any new workload is to run it next to the data, in whatever cloud the data already lives in. A compute job can be redeployed somewhere new in minutes. Moving the data itself means paying egress fees, waiting hours or days, and re-validating every downstream pipeline that depended on where it used to sit.

Here's the part that actually matters for architecture decisions: gravity frequently wins over stated strategy. A company can standardize on Azure, have Azure DevOps pipelines and Azure-trained staff, and still watch new analytics workloads land in AWS instead — because forty terabytes of transactional data has been accumulating in S3 for six years, and nobody's paying to move it just to satisfy a standardization goal. The real question to ask isn't 'what's our cloud preference' — it's 'where will this data's gravity actually be in two years,' and that question deserves an answer the moment a dataset first lands somewhere, not after a workload is already struggling against it.

So treat a new large dataset's landing zone as a long-lived architectural commitment, default to bringing compute to data rather than the reverse, and replicate only the subset that genuinely needs to cross clouds rather than mirroring everything to preserve an abstract cloud-agnostic ideal. Next lesson picks up exactly there — once some data really does have to cross clouds, what replication actually looks like, and the consistency tradeoffs that come with it.
